Experts overwhelmingly agree that later start times improve attendance and grades.
A 2022 review of twelve district studies found that higher attendance followed later start times.
It is widely believed among experts that later start times improve attendance and grades.

questions.stem: A student arguing for rent limits writes: "The landlord association's own report calculates that median rent rose 38 percent in five years." What does citing the opposing group's report mainly accomplish?
questions.correct: It draws on a source the opposition trusts, making the increase harder to dismiss as the student's own framing.
distractors: It demonstrates that the student has weighed both sides and remains entirely unbiased.
It concedes that the landlord association's position on rent limits is correct.
It shifts responsibility for the claim onto the association, so the student need not interpret the number.
questions.why: Borrowing the opponent's credibility strengthens a figure without granting the opponent's argument; reading the move as a concession is the common error. The student still has to interpret the number.
options: It concedes that the landlord association's position on rent limits is correct.
It shifts responsibility for the claim onto the association, so the student need not interpret the number.
It demonstrates that the student has weighed both sides and remains entirely unbiased.
It draws on a source the opposition trusts, making the increase harder to dismiss as the student's own framing.

questions.stem: A student writes: "Two news outlets reported that the tower is safe, so the claim is well corroborated." Both articles, it turns out, quote the same developer's press release. What is the main weakness in the reasoning?
questions.correct: Two reports of one press release are a single source, so they do not corroborate each other.
distractors: News outlets are unreliable on safety questions, so the student should cite only the developer.
The student should have found a third article, since three sources are always stronger than two.
The claim is weakened because the outlets never interviewed residents of the tower.
questions.why: Independent confirmation requires separate origins; counting repetitions of one press release inflates the evidence. Simply adding a third article repeating the same release does not fix it.
options: Two reports of one press release are a single source, so they do not corroborate each other.
News outlets are unreliable on safety questions, so the student should cite only the developer.
The student should have found a third article, since three sources are always stronger than two.
The claim is weakened because the outlets never interviewed residents of the tower.

questions.stem: A student finds that a study favoring a new housing development was funded by the developer. Which sentence uses the study most fairly?
questions.correct: The developer-funded study reports lower infrastructure costs, a figure that should be checked against an independent estimate.
distractors: The study proves infrastructure costs will fall, since its data were collected on site.
The study should be ignored entirely, because a funder with a stake makes research worthless.
The developer's study found lower costs, which shows the developer cares about taxpayers.
questions.why: Naming the funder and seeking independent confirmation keeps a usable finding honest. Discarding the study outright overcorrects, and treating the funder's interest as goodwill is the opposite error.
options: The study should be ignored entirely, because a funder with a stake makes research worthless.
The developer-funded study reports lower infrastructure costs, a figure that should be checked against an independent estimate.
The developer's study found lower costs, which shows the developer cares about taxpayers.
The study proves infrastructure costs will fall, since its data were collected on site.

questions.stem: A consultant's report concludes that the merger "delivered substantial savings," but its own table shows annual costs rising from $4.1 million to $5.3 million. Which sentence uses the report most accurately?
questions.correct: The report's own figures show costs rising, which undercuts its conclusion that the merger saved money.
distractors: The merger delivered substantial savings, according to the consultant's report on the merger.
The report's table and its conclusion agree that costs fell after the merger was completed.
Because a paid consultant wrote the report, neither its table nor its conclusion can be trusted.
questions.why: Reading the data against the conclusion is the skill being tested. Citing the conclusion alone repeats the contradiction, and dismissing the whole report ignores usable figures.
options: The merger delivered substantial savings, according to the consultant's report on the merger.
The report's table and its conclusion agree that costs fell after the merger was completed.
The report's own figures show costs rising, which undercuts its conclusion that the merger saved money.
Because a paid consultant wrote the report, neither its table nor its conclusion can be trusted.

questions.stem: A student's only citation is a news article headlined "Salt Is Safe," which summarizes a nutrition study without quoting the researchers' conclusion. What should the student do before relying on the claim?
questions.correct: Locate the original study and check whether its conclusion matches the headline.
distractors: Cite the headline as written, since any published news article is a legitimate source.
Find a second news article covering the same study to confirm the headline's wording.
Quote the headline but add that news coverage of nutrition research is often unreliable.
questions.why: Headlines are typically written by editors rather than researchers, so the primary study is what tests whether the claim survives summary. A second summary of the same study may repeat the same distortion.
options: Cite the headline as written, since any published news article is a legitimate source.
Find a second news article covering the same study to confirm the headline's wording.
Quote the headline but add that news coverage of nutrition research is often unreliable.
Locate the original study and check whether its conclusion matches the headline.

questions.stem: Arguing that a factory polluted the river, a student quotes a longtime resident: "I've lived here fifty years and I surely miss the old diner." What is the main problem with using this quotation as evidence?
questions.correct: It is memorable but says nothing about pollution, so it does not support the claim.
distractors: It is only one resident's view, so a statement from a second resident would fix the problem.
It is a direct quotation, so it needs a page citation before it can count as evidence.
Its nostalgic tone is too emotional for an academic argument, which should avoid feeling.
questions.why: Evidence must bear on the claim; a vivid quote about a diner shows nothing about the river. Adding a second irrelevant quotation, or flattening the tone, would not make it relevant.
options: It is memorable but says nothing about pollution, so it does not support the claim.
It is a direct quotation, so it needs a page citation before it can count as evidence.
It is only one resident's view, so a statement from a second resident would fix the problem.
Its nostalgic tone is too emotional for an academic argument, which should avoid feeling.
